cards.a: IPv6 is a 128-bit addressing scheme providing roughly 3.4 × 10^38 addresses. It solves IPv4 exhaustion, removes the need for NAT in most designs, and provides automatic link-local addressing, SLAAC, and no broadcast.

cards.q: How is an IPv6 address written?
cards.a: As eight groups of four hexadecimal digits (hextets), each group being 16 bits, for a total of 128 bits. Example: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334.

cards.q: What are the IPv6 shortening rules?
cards.a: Drop leading zeros in each group and replace the longest run of zero groups with :: exactly once. Example: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334 becomes 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334.

cards.q: What is an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address?
cards.a: An IPv6 address that embeds an IPv4 address in the final 32 bits, written like ::ffff:192.168.1.1 with the prefix ::ffff:0:0/96.

cards.q: What are the IPv6 prefixes for global unicast, link-local, unique local, and multicast?
cards.a: Global unicast is 2000::/3, link-local is fe80::/10, unique local is fc00::/7 (commonly seen as fd), and multicast is ff00::/8.

cards.q: What are the IPv6 loopback and unspecified addresses?
cards.a: Loopback is ::1 and the unspecified address is ::.

cards.q: What prefix identifies an anycast address?
cards.a: None: anycast uses the same address space as unicast, so it cannot be distinguished by prefix; any unicast address can be assigned to multiple nodes as an anycast address.

cards.q: How does IPv6 replace broadcast and ARP?
cards.a: IPv6 has no broadcast; broadcast is replaced by multicast (for example, all-nodes ff02::1) and ARP is replaced by Neighbor Discovery (ND). Routers do not fragment IPv6 packets; the sender performs Path MTU Discovery.

cards.q: What are the standard IPv6 subnetting units?
cards.a: A /64 is one LAN subnet and is required for SLAAC; the lower 64 bits are the interface ID (EUI-64 or random for privacy). Common allocations are /48 per site and /64 per VLAN, with providers assigning /56 to /48.

cards.q: What Linux host commands view IPv6 addressing?
cards.a: ip -6 addr show to view IPv6 addresses, ip -6 route for the IPv6 routing table, and ping6 2001:db8::1 to ping over IPv6.

cards.q: How do you configure IPv6 on a Cisco IOS interface?
cards.a: Use ipv6 address 2001:db8:1:10::1/64 for a static GUA, optionally ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local for a manual link-local address, or ipv6 enable to autoconfigure only a link-local address.

cards.q: What commands verify IPv6 on Cisco IOS?
cards.a: show ipv6 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 and show ipv6 route.

cards.q: Can an IPv6 address contain two double colons?
cards.a: No. The :: notation may appear only once, because two double colons would make the number of zero groups ambiguous and the address invalid.
No, 2001:db8:: is the documentation prefix defined in RFC 3849 and must not be used in production networks.

cards.q: Does a link-local address need to be configured manually?
cards.a: No. A fe80::/10 link-local address is automatically present on every IPv6-enabled interface; configuring one manually is always optional.

cards.q: Can SLAAC work on a /127 IPv6 subnet?
cards.a: No. SLAAC requires a /64 subnet; a /127 or /128 prefix breaks automatic address configuration.

cards.q: Is there such a thing as an IPv6 broadcast address?
cards.a: No. IPv6 has no broadcast; asking for the IPv6 broadcast address is a trick question, and broadcast-like traffic uses multicast such as ff02::1.

cards.q: How many hex digits does an IPv6 address contain?
cards.a: 32 hex digits arranged as 8 groups of 4.
